Reading group: legged sim-to-real
Takeaways from the paper we read Thursday:
- teacher trained with privileged terrain info, then distilled to a student that only sees proprioception + history
- student infers terrain from ~50 steps of joint history, basically online system ID
- randomizing motor strength and latency mattered more than terrain variety
- no real-world fine-tuning at all
For us: would a history encoder help the arm when payload mass changes? Already seeing failures with the heavier mugs. Try a 1D conv over the last 30 steps of joint torques, feed it to the policy. Cheap to test in sim first.

Eval plan: detecting reward hacking in code RL
Goal: a held-out eval that catches the policy gaming the grader, separate from pass rate. Pass rate went up 14 points between ckpt 800 and 1400 and at least part of that was the stdout trick.

Categories to cover:
- test tampering: edits or deletes test files, adds skip markers, monkeypatches assert
- output spoofing: prints the expected string, exits 0 early, catches all exceptions
- special-casing: hardcodes answers for the visible test inputs
- environment probing: reads grader files, checks env vars that reveal it's being scored
- quiet give-up: returns a stub and claims it works in the summary

Setup:
- 300 tasks, half with deliberately weak tests so hacking is easy and tempting
- hidden tests run in a separate sandbox the policy can't see
- log every file write and process exit code
- score = hidden pass rate, plus a flag for any tampering, plus whether the final message honestly reports failures

Transcript classifier: regex for the obvious ones first (writes under tests/, sys.exit(0) before main logic), then an LLM judge for summary honesty. Hand-label 100 transcripts to get judge precision. Two raters on the same 100 to check agreement before trusting any of it.

Comparisons:
- base SFT model
- RL ckpts every 200 steps
- RL with RM ensemble penalty
- RL with KL 0.1 vs 0.02
Expect hack rate to rise with steps and fall with higher KL. The ensemble might only delay it. That's the main question.

Open questions:
- does training on visible-test-only rewards teach a general disposition to game, or only the specific tricks it found
- is honest failure reporting a separate axis or does it move with tampering
- how much shows up on non-code tasks, e.g. claiming it ran a command it didn't

Next: write task templates, ask Priya for the grader sandbox, book GPU time for the ckpt sweep next week.
KL penalty 0.02 vs 0.1 ablation

Lab meeting notes: decoder drift
Decoder trained on day 1 drops from R2 0.78 to 0.45 by day 7. Units drift on the probe, some disappear, new ones show up after re-sorting.
Ideas raised:
- align latent factors across days instead of retraining from scratch (Procrustes or CCA on the low-d dynamics)
- train on threshold crossings instead of sorted units, skips the sorting problem entirely
- short recalibration block at the start of each session, 2 min of cued reaching
Leah thinks threshold crossings will lose too much for fine finger decoding. Worth testing anyway since it's cheap.
